orient: Narrator: Lockwood's diary at first. He has been ill at Thrushcross Grange for about four weeks since his snowy visits to Wuthering Heights in late 1801. After the row of asterisks Nelly Dean picks up her story again, about six months after Catherine's wedding to Edgar; scholars date the September evening she describes to 1783.

notes.t: A charming introduction to a hermit’s life
notes.g: Said sarcastically: a miserable start to his solitary life.
notes.n: In Chapter I Lockwood boasted that he had come north to get away from society. Now he has solitude, in a sickbed.
A 'surgeon' was a general country doctor, like Kenneth, not only someone who operated.

notes.g: Roads blocked by snow and mud.
Lack of human faces to look at.
notes.n: 'Dearth' means shortage; 'physiognomy' means face. Typical Lockwood: fancy words for 'I'm lonely'.

notes.g: Mr. Kenneth, the doctor from Gimmerton.
notes.n: He also appears in Nelly's story, attending the Earnshaws.

notes.g: Did me the honour of visiting me.
A pair of grouse, wild game birds of the moors.
notes.n: Grouse are shot from late summer into the winter, so these were among the last of the year.
Lockwood blames his illness on the freezing night and snowy walk of Chapters II and III, and on Heathcliff's poor hospitality.

notes.t: I had a great mind to tell him
notes.g: I very much wanted to tell him.

notes.t: pills and draughts, blisters and leeches
notes.g: The usual medical treatments of the day.
notes.n: A 'draught' was a dose of liquid medicine. 'Blisters' were plasters that raised blisters on the skin, thought to draw out illness. Leeches sucked blood, since bleeding was a standard cure.
Lockwood treats Nelly's story like a novel, with Heathcliff as hero and Catherine as heroine. Heathcliff vanished the night of the storm in Chapter IX.

notes.g: I'll ring the bell to call a servant.
notes.n: Rooms in a big house had bell-pulls connected to bells in the servants' quarters.

notes.g: Nelly (Ellen) Dean, Lockwood's housekeeper, who is telling the story.

notes.m: 'Wants' here means 'lacks', as in 'it wants ten minutes to six'. Nothing to do with wishing.

notes.g: Medicines sold as powders, stirred into water to drink.

notes.n: A phalanx is a tight battle formation of soldiers. Lockwood's mock-heroic joke about the bottles lined up by his bed.
Wealthy young Englishmen often finished their education by touring Europe (the 'Grand Tour').

notes.g: A poor student's place at university, paid for by doing servants' work.
notes.n: At Cambridge a sizar paid lower fees and got free food in return for menial duties.

notes.t: escape to America, and earn honours by drawing blood from his foster-country
notes.g: Go to America and win glory fighting against Britain, the country that raised him.
notes.n: The American War of Independence (1775–83) was being fought during the years Heathcliff was away.

notes.t: make a fortune more promptly on the English highways
notes.g: Get rich quicker as a highwayman, robbing travellers on the roads.
notes.n: Mounted highway robbers were still a real danger in the 1780s.

notes.g: Careers; ways of earning a living.

notes.t: I couldn’t give my word for any
notes.g: I couldn't swear to any of them.

notes.t: savage ignorance into which it was sunk
notes.g: The wild, uneducated state he had been pushed down into.
notes.n: Hindley had stopped Heathcliff's schooling and made him a farm labourer.

notes.m: 'Amuse' meant to pass the time pleasantly, not necessarily to make someone laugh.

notes.n: Nelly slips back into the name she used for her as a girl.

notes.g: To my pleasant surprise (I had expected worse).
The Lintons' house in the valley, where Lockwood is now a tenant.
Edgar Linton, Catherine's husband, now master of Thrushcross Grange.
notes.n: His parents died of the fever in Chapter IX, so 'Mr. Linton' now means Edgar.

notes.t: the thorn bending to the honeysuckles
notes.g: Catherine (the prickly thorn) did not give way to the gentle Lintons; they wrapped themselves round her.
notes.n: Honeysuckle is a climbing plant that twines around hedges such as hawthorn.

notes.g: Give and take on both sides.

notes.m: 'Humour' here means temper or mood, not comedy.

notes.t: never darkened on his own account
notes.g: He never frowned like that for his own sake.

notes.t: for the space of half a year
the gunpowder lay as harmless as sand
notes.g: Catherine's explosive temper stayed quiet, because nothing set it off.

notes.t: ascribed them to an alteration in her constitution
notes.g: Put them down to a change in her health.
notes.n: Your 'constitution' is your physical makeup and general health.
The fever she caught after Heathcliff disappeared (Chapter IX).

notes.t: we must be for ourselves in the long run
notes.g: In the end everyone looks after their own interests.

notes.t: the mild and generous are only more justly selfish than the domineering
notes.g: Gentle people are selfish too; they just have more right on their side than bullies.
notes.n: Nelly's view: Edgar's patience lasted only while Catherine put him first.

notes.g: The courtyard, enclosed by the house and its outbuildings.
A simple door fastening: a bar lifted by a small lever.
Hindley Earnshaw, Catherine's brother, master of Wuthering Heights.
notes.n: His father, old Mr. Earnshaw, is dead, so the title now belongs to Hindley.

notes.g: Black hair growing on his cheeks.
notes.m: Not a moustache: 'whiskers' meant hair on the cheeks, like long sideburns.

notes.g: Deep in their sockets and unusual.
notes.m: 'Singular' meant remarkable or strange, not 'single'.

notes.g: A living person, from this world.
notes.n: For a moment Nelly half wonders if he is a ghost.

notes.g: Twenty reflections of the moon (in the window panes).
notes.n: A 'score' is twenty.

notes.g: The nearest village, with the church and the doctor.

notes.t: put her out of her head
notes.g: Drive her out of her mind.

notes.t: Have you been for a soldier?
notes.g: Have you been in the army?
notes.n: Joining up as a common soldier was a usual way for a penniless young man to disappear.

notes.g: A hinged window of small panes in a criss-cross frame.
notes.n: Here it has been swung right open, back against the wall.

notes.g: The large private grounds of the Grange.
notes.m: A 'park' was the open land, grass and trees around a country house, not a public park.

notes.n: Where Catherine and Edgar were married (Chapter IX).

notes.g: A ditch or channel that drains water.
notes.n: Compare 'Gimmerden Sough' in Chapter III.

notes.t: Wuthering Heights rose above this silvery vapour
notes.g: The hilltop of Wuthering Heights showed above the mist.
notes.n: Here Nelly means the hill. The house itself sits just over the brow, out of sight from the Grange.

notes.g: Realising how foolish I was being.

notes.n: Not Edgar's mother, who died in Chapter IX.

notes.m: 'Directly' meant immediately, not 'in a straight line' or 'in a while'.
An 'apartment' meant a single room, not a flat.
'Carelessly' here means without concern, not clumsily.

notes.n: Heathcliff's dark looks had people calling him a gipsy since childhood (Chapter IV). Under Hindley he worked as a farm labourer.

notes.m: 'Sadly' here works like 'badly, very much'.

notes.n: In the Bible a 'jubilee' was a year of joy and freedom held every fiftieth year.

notes.g: Guessed that some terrible disaster had happened.

notes.t: suggested the kitchen as a more suitable place for him
notes.g: Edgar wants Heathcliff received in the kitchen, like a servant.
notes.n: Tradesmen and servants were seen in the kitchen; gentlefolk in the parlour.

notes.g: Nelly's proper first name (Nelly is a pet form of Ellen).

notes.n: She lives at the Grange with her brother. Nelly says below that she is eighteen.

notes.g: Since they are people of good family and rank.

notes.n: Catherine is mocking Edgar's snobbery.

notes.m: 'Arrest' just meant to stop or hold back, not to take into custody.

notes.g: Edgar's put-down: Heathcliff was a farmhand who walked out.
notes.n: Heathcliff left without warning the night of the storm (Chapter IX).

notes.m: 'Carriage' here means the way you hold your body, not a vehicle.

notes.t: retained no marks of former degradation
notes.g: Showed no trace of the humiliation and roughness of his past.

notes.m: 'Depressed' here means pressed down, low-set, not sad.

notes.t: at a loss how to address

notes.g: Like someone out of her mind with feeling.
Catherine's older brother, who treated Heathcliff cruelly after their father died.

notes.t: prevent the law by doing execution on myself
notes.g: Kill myself before the law could hang me (for killing Hindley).
notes.n: Murder was punished by hanging.

notes.t: She took her post before the urn
notes.g: She sat in her place to make and pour the tea.
notes.n: A tea urn was a large metal vessel of hot water with a tap, set on the tea table.

notes.t: The meal hardly endured ten minutes
notes.g: The meal barely lasted ten minutes.

notes.t: made a slop in his saucer
notes.n: A small sign of how rattled he is.

notes.g: Do harm in secret, behind a disguise.
A feeling that something bad is coming.
At the smallest upset or disappointment.
A strong dislike of each other.

notes.t: fancy the world was made for their accommodation
notes.g: Imagine the world exists to suit them.
Though I go along with both of them.
notes.m: To 'humour' someone is to give in to their wishes, nothing to do with being funny.
'Smart' here means sharp and stinging, not clever.
Again 'humour' means indulge, not amuse.

notes.g: Give in to their little passing wishes.
Foresee and supply everything you want.

notes.t: it would honour the first gentleman in the country
notes.g: Even the highest-ranking gentleman around would be honoured.
notes.n: 'The country' here means the district.

notes.t: quite a Christian: offering the right hand of fellowship to his enemies
notes.g: Nelly is being ironic: Heathcliff is making friends with his old enemy, as a good Christian should.
notes.n: The 'right hand of fellowship' is a Bible phrase (Galatians 2:9) for welcoming a partner. Jesus told his followers to love their enemies.

notes.g: The old, harshly religious servant at Wuthering Heights.
The man who used to torment him.
notes.m: 'Ancient' here just means former, from long ago, not very old.
'Liberal' meant generous, not anything political.

notes.g: To live at Wuthering Heights as a paying lodger.
Greed for money and what others have.

notes.t: what he grasps with one hand he flings away with the other
notes.g: He is greedy but also wasteful.

notes.t: a nice place for a young man to fix his dwelling in
notes.g: Said sarcastically: a terrible place for a young man to settle.
notes.n: Nelly means Hindley's drinking, gambling household.

notes.g: His cool, hard mind (also: he can hold his drink).

notes.t: reconciled me to God and humanity
notes.g: Made me feel at peace with God and the world again.

notes.n: 'Providence' means God's care and plan for the world.
'That creature' is Catherine's scornful name for her husband.

notes.t: cloud its removal with idle petulance
notes.g: Spoil the end of her misery with silly sulking.

notes.t: slap me on the cheek, I’d not only turn the other
notes.g: From Jesus's teaching to 'turn the other cheek' when struck.
notes.n: Matthew 5:39: 'whosoever shall smite thee on thy right cheek, turn to him the other also.'

notes.t: Mr. Heathcliff I should say in future
notes.g: From now on Nelly gives him the title 'Mr.'
notes.n: A sign of his new standing as a gentleman with money.

notes.t: estimating how far its owner would bear his intrusion
notes.g: Judging how much of his visiting Edgar would put up with.

notes.t: established his right to be expected
reserve for which his boyhood was remarkable
notes.g: The silent, closed-off manner he was known for as a boy.

notes.t: diverted it into another channel for a space
notes.g: Turned his worry in a different direction for a while.

notes.m: 'Fantastic' meant based on fantasy, unreal, not 'excellent'.

notes.t: the degradation of an alliance with a nameless man
notes.g: The disgrace of a marriage to a man with no family name or background.
notes.n: Heathcliff was a foundling with only one name (Chapter IV). Family and rank mattered enormously in choosing a gentleman's sister's husband.
Estates usually passed to sons. If Edgar had none, the property could go to Isabella, and a married woman's property came under her husband's control.

notes.g: Drew back, dreading what might happen.
Handing Isabella over into its care.
Her love grew without his encouraging it.
Was not returned; he felt nothing for her.
Worried and wasted away with longing.
On the excuse that she was unwell.

notes.m: 'Peculiarly' means particularly, not oddly.

notes.g: In a commanding way that allowed no argument.

notes.n: A 'fondling' was someone petted and fussed over, a darling.

notes.g: Someone who won't let others have what they don't need themselves.
notes.n: From Aesop's fable: a dog lies in a manger of hay it cannot eat, and snarls to stop the ox from eating it.

notes.g: Long for Heathcliff to admire you.
A wild creature that has never been tamed.
notes.n: 'Unreclaimed' was used of wasteland never turned into farmland, and of wild hawks never trained.

notes.g: Without education or polish (and, like wild land, never farmed).

notes.t: arid wilderness of furze and whinstone
notes.g: A dry wasteland of gorse bushes and hard rock.
notes.n: Furze (gorse) is a spiny moorland shrub. Whinstone is a very hard dark rock.

notes.g: A person with a good heart under rough manners.

notes.t: a pearl-containing oyster of a rustic
notes.g: A country fellow with a treasure hidden inside.
Marrying you for your money and what you stand to inherit.
notes.n: 'Expectations' meant an inheritance you expect to receive.

notes.t: avarice is growing with him a besetting sin
notes.g: Greed is becoming the sin he keeps falling into.
notes.n: A 'besetting sin' comes from Hebrews 12:1, 'the sin which doth so easily beset us'.

notes.g: A sign of bad luck; someone who brings trouble.
notes.n: Birds such as ravens were thought to foretell disaster.

notes.g: Mortgaging his property: borrowing with his land as security.

notes.t: does nothing but play and drink
notes.g: Does nothing but gamble and drink.
notes.m: 'Play' here means gambling at cards and dice.

notes.e: flees afore to oppen t’ pikes!
notes.tr: We'll be having a coroner's inquest soon at our house. One of them nearly had his finger cut off holding the other back from sticking himself like a calf. That's the master, you know, who is so keen to go up before the great court of judgment. He's not afraid of the bench of judges, neither Paul, nor Peter, nor John, nor Matthew, nor any of them, not he! He positively likes, he longs, to set his brazen face against them! And that fine lad Heathcliff, you remember, he's a rare one. He can grin and laugh as well as anybody at a real devil's joke. Doesn't he ever say anything about his fine living among us when he goes to the Grange? This is how it goes: up at sunset; dice, brandy, closed shutters and candlelight till noon the next day. Then the fool goes cursing and raving to his room, making decent folk stick their fingers in their ears for very shame; and the rogue, why, he can count his money, and eat, and sleep, and go off to his neighbour's to gossip with the wife. Of course, he tells Dame Catherine how her father's gold runs into his pocket, and her father's son gallops down the broad road to ruin, while he runs ahead to open the toll gates!
notes.n: Joseph means that Hindley nearly stabbed himself, and that Heathcliff is taking Hindley's money while speeding him on to destruction.

notes.g: Coroner's inquest: an official inquiry into a sudden or violent death.
Stabbing himself like a calf being slaughtered.
The great assizes: Joseph's name for God's Last Judgment.
notes.n: The assizes were the courts where judges tried serious crimes. Joseph means Hindley is eager to die and face God's judgment.

notes.t: norther Paul, nur Peter, nur John, nur Matthew
notes.g: Neither Paul, nor Peter, nor John, nor Matthew.
notes.n: Joseph pictures the apostles as the judges on the bench at the Last Judgment. In Matthew 19:28 Jesus says the apostles will sit on thrones judging Israel.

notes.g: Grin or snarl, showing the teeth.

notes.n: 'Brass' is still northern English slang for money.

notes.g: Joseph's mock-grand title for Mrs. Linton (Catherine).

notes.n: From Matthew 7:13: 'broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction'.
Turnpikes were toll gates on main roads. Heathcliff, Joseph says, runs ahead to clear Hindley's road to ruin.

notes.g: In league with the others; on their side.
Lies told to damage someone's reputation.
Ill will; a wish to do harm.

notes.t: a justice-meeting at the next town
notes.g: A meeting of local magistrates in the nearest town.
notes.n: Gentleman landowners served as unpaid magistrates, or justices of the peace, as Edgar's father did (Chapter VI).

notes.g: A brief burst of strong feeling.
Sweeping the stone floor in front of the fireplace.

notes.m: 'Sadly' here means 'badly, very much'.

notes.t: It lies in your own power to be Edgar’s brother
notes.g: You could become Edgar's brother-in-law by marrying Isabella.
Holding her back, pretending to be playful.
notes.m: 'Arresting' here means stopping someone, not a police arrest.
'Confounded' here means confused and abashed, not the mild curse word.

notes.t: shoot a shaft into your soul
notes.g: Shoot an arrow into your heart, like Cupid.

notes.m: 'Intimate' just meant close and familiar, with no sexual sense.
To 'entertain' a feeling is to hold it in your mind, not to amuse.

notes.g: You misrepresent her; you tell lies about her.

notes.n: 'The Indies' meant the East or West Indies: faraway hot countries full of strange creatures.

notes.t: ornamented the detainer’s with crescents of red
notes.g: Decorated Catherine's hand with red half-moon marks from her nails.

notes.n: A vixen is a female fox, and also a word for a bad-tempered woman.

notes.g: Claws, as of a bird of prey.
Weapons that can do real damage.
Gruesome, like a ghoul (a grave-robbing demon).

notes.t: painting on its white the colours of the rainbow
notes.g: Covering her pale face with bruises.
notes.n: A brutal joke: he means he would beat her, 'turning the blue eyes black'.
From the Song of Solomon 1:15: 'thou hast doves' eyes'.

notes.g: Will she inherit her brother's property?
notes.n: Edgar has no children yet, so for now Isabella stands next in line.

notes.t: Half a dozen nephews shall erase her title
notes.g: I'll have sons who will come before her in the inheritance.
notes.n: Catherine means children of her own with Edgar, who would be Isabella's nephews. 'Title' means her legal claim.

notes.t: Abstract your mind from the subject
notes.g: Take your mind off the subject.
Want what belongs to someone else.
notes.n: From the Ten Commandments (Exodus 20:17): 'Thou shalt not covet thy neighbour's house... nor any thing that is thy neighbour's'.

notes.t: they would be none the less that
notes.g: They would still be just as much yours.

notes.t: My heart invariably cleaved to the master’s
notes.g: My sympathy always stuck to the master's side.
notes.n: 'Cleave' here means cling.

notes.g: A lot of freedom in how she behaved.
Hindley, pictured as a lost sheep.
notes.n: Bible imagery: Jesus as the good shepherd who goes looking for the lost sheep (Luke 15).

notes.t: an evil beast prowled between it and the fold
notes.g: Heathcliff is the wolf lurking between the sheep and safety.
notes.n: A 'fold' is a pen for sheep. Here it stands for God's protection.
